newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Germany says exports fuelled economic growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Germany says exports fuelled economic growth.

text.p: Germany, Europe's economic locomotive, stayed on the growth track in the third quarter but its recovery was still driven by foreign orders while domestic investment lagged, the economics ministry said on Wednesday.

German gross domestic product (GDP) probably rose two percent in real terms in the third quarter from the same period a year ago after year-on-year expansion of 1.2 percent in the second quarter, the ministry said in its latest monthly report.

While continued weak domestic investment offered little hope to Germany's four million jobless, steady growth should be good news for the government's efforts to meet the strict targets for Europe's single currency.

"The driving force behind economic expansion was foreign stimulus after the middle of the year," the report said. "In addition to a more dynamic world economy, the improvements in the competitiveness of German producers had a positive effect."
The economy also expanded on a quarter-on-quarter basis, but the rate of growth eased from unexpectedly strong growth of 1.5 percent in the previous quarter.
The ministry said this was not surprising because the second quarter had been marked by "normalisation of economic activity after the cold winter."

Independent economists said the figures showed the recovery was still intact but expressed concern that the growth estimate came so soon after the release of weak September industrial output and orders data which were still due to be revised.
Economists said they expected growth of up to one percent for the third quarter compared to the previous three months.

"We had an exhorbitant growth rate in the second quarter compared with the previous quarter - mainly because of a catch-up effect after the harsh winter," said Adolf Rosenstock at the Industrial Bank of Japan in Frankfurt. "This could not be repeated in the third quarter."
The Federal Statistics Office will release third quarter growth data early next month.
The figures also showed that economic growth this year could reach as much 1.5 percent, above government forecasts of 0.75 percent to 1.0 percent.

German exports have been rising as a result of improved competitiveness of German companies, helped by the mark's weakening against major currencies, this year's moderate wage agreements and corporate restructuring. But there is little stimulus for economic growth from domestic spending.
After a strong rise in the second quarter of the year, domestic manufacturing orders fell in the third quarter by two percent from the same period a year ago on an adjusted basis.
"This is of particular concern because investment activity decisively influences the room for broad economic growth and employment in the coming years," the ministry said.
Taking a closer look at the economy, the report said the manufacturing sector looked bright, with output up slightly in the third quarter from the previous quarter.

Capacity usage at German factories was up, though still below normal levels. The construction industry was marked by a lack of momentum. Private spending, based on retail sales data which account for 40 percent of private consumption, was weak.
The government expressed concern about developments in east Germany, still recovering from decades of communism.
A sharp decline in building activity in the eastern states has not been offset by increased output in other sectors. Growth in the manufacturing sector was particularly moderate.

"The east German economy will therefore probably not grow noticeably faster this year than the west German," the ministry said. "Efforts to catch up (with the west) are therefore beginning to falter."
